Lade
LAYD
verb
From the Old English hladan, “to load, to heap up, to draw”; hence to load, to burden, to lay a weight upon a beast or a back. Its past is laded and its participle laden.

Biblical Definition

To lade is to load — to lay a burden on a beast or a back. Most often it is honest labour: “Lade your beasts, and go, get you unto the land of Canaan” (Gen 45:17), says Pharaoh, and the asses go out heaped with the good things of Egypt to a famished father. Nehemiah saw men “lading asses” on the sabbath and testified against them, for the day of God is not a day for loading. But Scripture soon turns the word inward, from the beast’s back to the soul’s. Isaiah cries, “Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity” (Isa 1:4) — guilt is a freight, and a nation staggers under it. And our Lord lays the word like a whip across the shoulders of the religious: “Woe unto you also, ye lawyers! for ye lade men with burdens grievous to be borne, and ye yourselves touch not the burdens with one of your fingers” (Luk 11:46). That is the whole indictment of legalism in one sentence — men who pile the load and will not lift a finger under it, who bind on consciences what God never bound, and who are heavy with rules and light with mercy. Over against every such lader stands the Saviour, whose call is not to load but to unload: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Mat 11:28). The scribes lade; Christ unlades. His yoke is easy and His burden is light, because He carried the weight Himself.

Webster 1828 Definition

To load; to burden; to lay a weight upon a beast or a back; participle laden.

expand to see more

LADE, to load; to put on a burden; to charge with a freight.

From the Saxon hladan, “to load, to heap, to draw.”

Past laded; participle laden, as a people laden with iniquity (Isa 1:4).

The lawyers laded men with burdens grievous to be borne (Luk 11:46).

Christ calls the heavy laden to Himself for rest (Mat 11:28).

Key Scripture

Gen 45:17 — "And Pharaoh said unto Joseph, Say unto thy brethren, This do ye; lade your beasts, and go, get you unto the land of Canaan;"

Isa 1:4 — "Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, a seed of evildoers, children that are corrupters: they have forsaken the LORD, they have provoked the Holy One of Israel unto anger, they are gone away backward."

Luk 11:46 — "And he said, Woe unto you also, ye lawyers! for ye lade men with burdens grievous to be borne, and ye yourselves touch not the burdens with one of your fingers."

Mat 11:28 — "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."

Modern Corruption

A live corruption, and an old one: the lawyers lade men with burdens God never laid, and touch them not with one of their fingers.

expand to see more

The woe our Lord pronounced on the lawyers is the standing rebuke of legalism in every age. They laded men with burdens grievous to be borne — hedges about the law, traditions with the force of commandments, scruples multiplied until religion became a freight no back could carry — and touched not the burdens with one of their fingers. That is the mark of the false teacher: he is rigorous with other men’s consciences and lenient with his own. Wherever a church binds where God has not bound, whether by ceremony, by rule, or by the private standards of the strong pressed upon the weak, it has taken up the lawyer’s trade and laded the flock it was called to feed.

The corruption has a mirror image, and it is no better: the teacher who lifts every burden God did lay, and calls the unlading grace. Isaiah’s nation was laden with iniquity and did not know it, and the man who tells a laden sinner he carries nothing has not eased him but blinded him. The gospel does not deny the weight; it removes it, and only Christ can. He alone says, Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest — for the burden the lawyers piled on other men, and the guilt Isaiah’s people staggered under, He took upon Himself and bore up the hill to Calvary. His yoke is easy because He carried the load.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means to load, to burden, to lay a weight upon a beast or a back.

expand to see more

Lade — Old English hladan, “to load, to heap, to draw.”

It denotes laying a freight or burden upon a beast or a man.

Its participle is laden, as a people laden with iniquity (Isa 1:4).

The lawyers lade men with burdens they will not touch (Luk 11:46).

Christ unlades the heavy laden and gives them rest (Mat 11:28).

Usage

"Lade your beasts and go: the asses went out heaped with the good things of Egypt."

"Ye lade men with burdens grievous to be borne, and touch them not with one finger."

"The scribes lade and Christ unlades: come unto me, all ye that are heavy laden."
